raw_case_text:
A 20-year-old former healthy Iranian woman referred to our tertiary clinic with acute, sharp epigastric pain and vomiting. The patient gave a history of similar pain episodes, which resulted in referring to other emergency departments and received conservative treatment. Other than this was unremarkable. She denied weight loss or diarrhea and had no jaundice. On general physical examination, there were no significant points. Her family history was negative for relevant gastrointestinal malignancies.
On admission, routine laboratory tests, including complete blood count, liver function test, electrolytes, venous blood gas, blood sugar, urine analysis, and urine culture, were within a normal range. Except for mild anemia, no other things were seen. With doubt of any gynecologic pathologies such as ectopic pregnancy, beta-human chorionic gonadotropin (BHCG) was measured, which was unremarkable.
In the emergency department, complete abdomen and pelvic ultrasound (U/S) were requested, which showed a hypoechoic lesion with 8 x 8 cm size with a probable pancreatic origin and suggested a CT scan with and without contrast to be more accurate.
Abdominal contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CECT) scan revealed a 7.5 x 7 hypodense mass in the epigastric area between the liver, kidney, and pancreas. Also, a 5 cm simple splenic cyst was reported (Figure 1). It suggested an evaluation of the hydatid cyst. Hence, hydatidAb (IgG) was requested which was negative.
In an attempt to clarify the diagnosis, EUS was performed and found a 9 x 7.5 cm heterogeneous well-defined mass lesion with possible belonging to neck of pancreas (NOP) and portal vein (PV) confluence compression, so the pancreatic solid pseudopapillary neoplasm was the most likely diagnosis. A Whipple's procedure and partial splenectomy were planned. The preoperative and postoperative periods were uneventful. The patient was discharged after eight days with acetaminophen 325 mg TDS, ranitidine BID, and ferrous sulfate plus folic acid daily as well as recommended to refer to the outpatient clinic for post-op observation. The surgical specimen was sent to pathology; macroscopically, the head of the pancreas with the greatest dimension of 7 cm encapsulated with a solid, hemorrhagic, and necrotic area was described. Microscopically as shown in Figure 2, the lesion was composed of a well-circumscribed encapsulated neoplasm with solid and pseudopapillary components and large areas of necrosis. The neoplastic cells were mildly pleomorphic epithelial cells with round to oval nuclei, some with grooves and indistinctive nuclei with low mitotic activity, and pale acidophilic to clear cytoplasms. Some tumoral cells contained hyaline globules within their cytoplasms. The areas of cystic degeneration with cholesterol crystals and foamy histiocytes were observed as well. Immunohistochemical study revealed immunoreactivity for vimentin, progesterone, and beta-catenin in tumoral cells while they were negative for cytokeratin, chromogranin, synaptophysin, and CD99 (Figure 3).
The patient's postoperative recovery was smooth, and she was well without complications or signs of recurrence at five months follow-up.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 20-year-old Iranian woman presented with acute, sharp epigastric pain and vomiting.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The previously healthy patient presented to the tertiary clinic with acute sharp epigastric pain accompanied by vomiting, noting prior similar episodes of epigastric pain managed conservatively at outside emergency departments.
subjective.past_medical_history: Previously healthy; negative family history for gastrointestinal malignancies.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for acute sharp epigastric pain and vomiting; negative for weight loss, diarrhea, or jaundice.

objective.physical_examination: General and systemic physical examinations were unremarkable.
objective.routine_investigations: Routine blood tests showed mild anemia with normal WBC, liver function tests, electrolytes, venous blood gas, blood glucose, urinalysis, urine culture, and serum beta-hCG. Serum Echinococcus IgG antibody was negative. Abdominopelvic ultrasound identified an 8 x 8 cm hypoechoic epigastric lesion of probable pancreatic origin.
objective.advanced_workup: Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT demonstrated a 7.5 x 7 cm hypodense mass in the epigastrium between the liver, kidney, and pancreas along with a 5-cm simple splenic cyst. Endoscopic ultrasound (EUS) revealed a well-defined 9 x 7.5 cm heterogeneous mass arising from the neck of the pancreas and compressing the portal vein confluence. Following a Whipple procedure (pancreaticoduodenectomy) and partial splenectomy, pathology of the 7-cm encapsulated solid-hemorrhagic-necrotic pancreatic head/neck tumor showed solid and pseudopapillary proliferations of mildly pleomorphic epithelial cells with nuclear grooves, hyaline cytoplasmic globules, cholesterol crystals, and foamy histiocytes; IHC was positive for vimentin, progesterone receptor, and beta-catenin and negative for cytokeratin, chromogranin, synaptophysin, and CD99.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Solid pseudopapillary neoplasm (SPN / Frantz tumor) of the pancreas accompanied by a simple splenic cyst, confirmed by EUS, Whipple resection histopathology, and vimentin/progesterone-receptor/beta-catenin immunohistochemical positivity after hydatid cyst was excluded by negative Echinococcus IgG serology. The patient was discharged on postoperative day 8 and remained asymptomatic without recurrence at 5-month follow-up.
